utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I was advised that the accused has something to raise in the absence of the witness, but for the sake of saving time in the future, I would like the witness to be inside the courtroom always and then parties would -- who wishes to raise something in the absence of the witness should communicate to the Legal Officer and the Chamber in advance. Okay. That said, I'll hear what Mr. Karadzic has to say. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. I will try to be as concise as possible. First of all, I would like to express my high esteem and appreciation for your assistance and the tips you gave me for examination. However, there are two underlying technical things. At the outset, I accepted all the electronic material, a million and 3.000 pages plus 700.000 of my own, which makes 2 million. I'm afraid that the technical capacities at my disposal do not keep up with the scope of this process. Furthermore, Lord Bonomy ordered in the summer last year and OLAD promised that I would receive my own server, which would make it easier for me. However, I got access to the server only last Sunday. For the past two days, I did not have my computer with me because they were putting data in. This morning, I did not have time to get the documents from the computer that I know I need for this witness. I appreciate greatly your patience with my imperfect skills of examination, but I have to say that this is a very well-trained witness whose many statements have long been polished by the Prosecution, and I am at a disadvantage here because the witness is not unbiassed and honest. He is very biassed and very insincere. He is a direct participant, and he is clearly inclined to avoid many of my questions and let his statements stand as facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We accept the procedural mechanism of occasional and necessary oral submissions pertaining to issues that arise during the course of these proceedings. We do not accept argument about the witnesses, particularly unfounded argument, I would add. If the -- secondly, if the accused has a motion to make, the opportunity for oral submissions presented by Court should not supplant the written procedure which give rise to the opportunity for considered review, timely responses by the Prosecution, and so on. So I want to urge at the outset the avoidance of replacement mechanisms for the procedures which are well embedded in this institution for making submissions. But again, more importantly, I want to discourage argumentation in the guise of procedural submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. While I understand your concerns, I did let it go because he's rather concentrating his submission on the procedural issues than his submission as to the credibility of the witness himself. But bearing that in mind, Mr. Karadzic, so what is your point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I see that you fully understand where I'm going, and I believe this intervention by my learned friend Mr. Tieger is quite unnecessary. I did not wish to discredit this witness. I just wanted to indicate how I will be working as I continue this cross-examination and why I will be working that way. Yesterday, you quite rightly asked me where I was going when I was asking about the names of various people or his grandchildren. I have to say now that this is a witness who will keep trying to wriggle, and I have to be persistent and I have to try to stop him from wriggling out of my questions and get to the truth. This is just an explanation of how I intend to proceed from now on. I will present today, in keeping with the tips given me by Judge Morrison yesterday, certain statements and I will ask the witness to say: Yes, no, or I don't know. And I will not have time to discredit that today or refute it, but during the trial I will refute it because there are certain truths that no one can change, and they throw a completely different light on what the witness has said so far in his multiple statements. That is all I wanted to say. I will make certain statements. Please say: Yes, no, or I don't know, because his statements are full of lump-sum claims, and if I do not prove that they are ungrounded and false, they can later serve as grounds for a conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, even if you are minded to challenge the credibility of the witness, the Chamber is of the view that you do not need all that time you indicated yesterday. You -- of course you have ample opportunity to bring your witnesses during the Defence case. You don't have to put every point to the witness to challenge the credibility of the witness if you concentrate on real issues. Given that the Prosecution spent about an hour and 20 minutes yesterday and you spent about approximately one hour and 40 minutes and also given that you indicated you would need four hours to cross-examine this witness, the Chamber is of the view that you do not need more than an hour and a half from now to finish this witness. So given -- bearing in mind that the advocacy lesson you had yesterday. So try to concentrate on real issues. So that said, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope you had a good night, a good rest. I'd like to remind you of the oath you took yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will seek to present to you the view of the Defence on certain points and see if you can answer with yes, no, or I don't know; and please understand that I'm not accusing you of anything at any point. I'm just trying to find out what you know about certain things and what you can testify. Yesterday, we left off with a claim made by Muslim commanders to the author Zilhad Kljucanin that they had had difficulty mobilising fighting men at the time because a large number of them believed that there will be no conflict and that Serbs would do them no harm. And when they formed that armed unit in Mahala, it was their problem and you said you were among those who believed there would not be a conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would be only too happy to believe you, but my problem is that you acquired a machine-gun which is not really a hunting weapon and you did not turn it over. And there was a point when you took up position at a graveyard behind that machine-gun, but you did not fire because you said the Serbs would then return and fire back.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I laid down on the ground in that Muslim cemetery, that nobody shot at the Serbs because the Serbs would have returned and killed the entire village, and that's true; which means I didn't use the gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you took up that position, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I laid down on the ground behind my machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that explosives were found in your home, explosives that may have originated from your mine? Doesn't that work contrary to your claim that you believed there would be no conflict?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then call up a statement in e-court. Defence document 1D29. While we're waiting -- oh, here the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Djordje Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was he by position, occupation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't he have a concession on the mine where you worked?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say yesterday, and you said so in your statement as well, that because of the turnout of Serbs to the mobilisation call of the JNA, only non-Serbs remained to work in the mine because the Serbs had gone to Croatia to fight?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that yesterday. It was in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you refuse to go to Croatia to fight?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But were you asked, or rather, called up to military drills in the past?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were other Muslim reservists called up to drills in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the war in Croatia, were they called up to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hoping you would ask that question. I can't wait to answer. Yes, in June 1991, all reservists were called up between Ostra Luka and Koprivna, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike, and they were supposed to go, as they put it, to the theatre of war in Croatia. However, when the supply of weapons ran out, and I think it was a certain Captain Zeljaja who took the weapons, then the Muslims abandoned the drill, this military exercise. And then the Serbs were sent to the theatre of war, some to Vukovar, some to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it means that the Muslims did not respond to that mobilisation call up?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Captain Zeljaja, was he in the military chain of command of the JNA? Was he an active-duty officer?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was mainly stationed in Prijedor, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leaving aside your comment that he could have distributed or taken some weapons, if he had been ordered to do so by his chain of command he had to do it. In any case, the Serbs went to war instead of working in the mine?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many Muslims and Croats remained in the mine?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the production went on?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the statement of Mr. Djordje Todorovic obtained by my investigator.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, just say: I confirm, I deny, or I don't know. In peacetime, even without any goings on on the front line, the ethnic composition in the mine where he owned a concession was Muslims 60 per cent, Croats 10 per cent, and Serbs 30 per cent; and when these Serbs went to the front line, Muslims and Croats made up 100 per cent; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He had two open-pit mines?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was one deep mine and you were the manager?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could both of you kindly put a pause between the question and answer, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree or do you deny that the technical director was Zijad Okanovic, who was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that. He was the technical director.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the production manager in the pit Salim, I don't know his last name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man with the last name of Strbac was, in fact, on that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But Salim was in a senior position. Was the manager of the open-cast mine Alija Plavnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he worked there, but whether he was a lawyer or a manager, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he was in an executive position, not a worker?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Zdenka, a Croat, also in a managing position?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a little. What Zdenka was by ethnicity, as I said yesterday, I didn't go in such things, and we didn't really know each other by ethnicity. We valued each other for personal qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the chief of accounting Mr. Raif, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the chief of commercial affairs Enisa Vajzovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know she was chief of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Was she a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can determine by name, you and I, but the Chamber cannot.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that you were called by the secretary of the manager of the mine and told you not to come to work for a while. But she didn't give you a letter of dismissal, just told you not to come to work for a while?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it Sanja Grapcanovic, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was Zdenka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was Zdenka, the one we mentioned a moment ago. Let's see what it says further on. In point 8, Mr. Todorovic says all the other lower-ranking executives were also occupying their positions only because of their professional qualifications, not because of ethnic background, as proved by this list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the picture of the work force shows that it wasn't important who was of which faith?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get the next page of this document. This is page 3. Is that how it should be? Is there a page 2? This is page 3. Then please, let's see the previous page but the bottom of the previous page which we did not see, item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you see item 9 says: "The aforesaid Zulic, Ahmet, was not arrested because he was an employee of the Kamengrad mine but for other reasons. To my recollection, a certain quantity of explosives ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... a certain quantity of explosives and one machine-gun were found on him. The explosive that was found originated from the Kamengrad mine." What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you claim about this explosive is a pure lie because, first of all, I have to say this to the Chamber and explain. You could not just come in and take explosives because it was very well kept in a special depot for explosives. And in 1992, this depot was controlled by the JNA and the Serbs. So unless you were an authorised worker, the one who needed explosives for his work in the mine - and even they, when using explosives, had to explain and report exactly how many bores they had made with that explosives and they had to count and report the number of fuses that had to be retrieved. So you could not easily get access to explosives and take it out of the mine even in peacetime, let alone in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I can believe that this used to be so before all the Serbs went to the front line, but what was it like when only Muslims and Croats remained in the mine, who then controlled the depot?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA and the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were in the mine?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not in the mine. They were by the depot of explosives, and the depot of explosives was in a place called Dolnica [phoen]. It had five circles of wire fence around it, and it was guarded by Serb policemen and then JNA. So there was not even a theoretical possibility to take explosives out for that reason. I just want to say that the person who wrote this is a liar. The submachine-gun that I acquired is the truth and I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any people who worked with explosives?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Milos Strbac, Mirsad Burnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Any more?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all of them now, but there were ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Mirsad, was he related to Enver, the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they're from the same family and the same last name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they lived 7 kilometres from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I notice that you are overriding the interpretation of the answer given by the witness. Please put a pause after the answer. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I want us to get through this as quickly as possible, so that's why I'm speeding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us any other names of people working with explosives and could set off mines and explosives, especially when the Serbs were not there. Who worked with the explosives then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who worked on the open-cast mines with the explosives, but I know that there was just Mile, and Mirsad, Mile Strbac and Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, you said yesterday that your brother worked in Kamengrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he stayed on there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He worked there until when?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the end of 1995 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the end of the war, until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not the whole time. Until August 1995, that's how long he worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in point 11, Mr. Todorovic says here: "I state that no one fired Ahmet Zulic from the company because of his nationality and by helping his mother, I ignored that at that moment." Well, actually, I want to refer to point 10. It says: "Their mother suffers a stroke and they turned to me for help during the war. I personally drove their mother to the hospital in Prijedor for treatment, which goes to show my way of thinking, both then and now." Did your mother have a stroke during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did she have any trouble with her blood pressure or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I want to say is this: Before the war my father was -- well, had a stroke in 1981, but not my mother. My mother never suffered a stroke and he never drove her. I know Djordje personally, and I'd like to see him so I can tell him that he's lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, tell me this, please, you said yesterday that you had three brothers?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they in the Betonirka firm or at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are they Muslims like you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's why they were expelled, the two brothers were expelled in convoys. When the mop-up operation took place, they left with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that, but you said that it was difficult to leave Sanski Most. So they left at their own request, but let's leave that aside for the moment.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't put words into my mouth and say that I said it was difficult to leave Sanski Most; that's not what I said. I didn't say it was difficult to leave Sanski Most. That was the easiest thing in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I'd like to refer to the paragraph of your statement where you said that your wife had difficulties in obtaining permits to leave Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, she did. And let me explain, Your Honours, why she had difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've refrained from doing it until this point, but can the accused please give the page number and the paragraph number in the amalgamated statement that he's referring to, or if he's referring to one of the witness's previous statements or transcript, can he give that statement and then the page number in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could give the para numbers, as Ms. Sutherland indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would have done that had I expected the witness to expand on his statements and views with respect to the difficulties and the persecution from Sanski Most. We know that in Sanski Most - and you'll see this in the transcript, that the witness confirmed this, and let me just find that part of the statement. I would have prepared this had I known that he was going to deal with the departure from Sanski Most, but I will find the paragraph by the end of my cross-examination. He says that his wife had a great deal of problems in obtaining what she needed to leave Sanski Most, and we have evidence of that. In the whole of Bosanska Krajina, they had to have a lot of papers and permits and certificates in order to leave. It is paragraph 40 -- 140 for everybody's benefit. So let's see what it says in paragraph 140. This is what it says: [In English] "In December 1992, my wife decided to leave Sanski Most municipality. She thought I had been killed. She wanted to get out -- of our four children out of -- because the house have been attacked. In order to do this, she first had to go to Sanski Most municipality authorities to sign a statement renouncing her house to the municipality to the authorities. She had to pay all the utilities. She had to go to the re-settlement authorities in Sanski Most for a receipt that she had signed off to the Serb authorities all her property. A Serb friend of the family came to Sanski Most and took my wife and children to his house in Banja Luka. In order to leave Banja Luka, she had to pay money to the Bureau for Resettlement which was run by the Serb authorities. She said two amounts: 22.000 dinars for bureau expeditious and 175.000 dinars for the transport costs. However, she still had to pay for bus fare. She had copies of the renouncement documents, however, in Bosanska Gradiska the 'customs officers' took her possessions from her including her documents," and so on, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zulic, your wife informed you that she had many obstacles to surmount and difficulties to leave. Not only was she not expelled, but she was discouraged to do so with all these different procedures by the authorities, and I go into this only because you've expanded on what you've said.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not expand on what I've said, Your Honours. I have to explain this situation. The Serbs organised convoys going out of Sanski Most, and men, women, children, they would get into those convoys and leave. However, those people who did not have, just like me, I was detained by those Serb Chetnik authorities. So people who didn't have a chance to leave and she didn't have a chance to leave in the convoy because the convoys were checked. And then finally, she had to pay all this money, go around looking for permits, because there was great pressure on her to leave. So my brothers had no problems because the Serbs organised the departure, if you remember my talking about that, the departure of non-Serbs from Mahala and Muhic to Kladusa. And that's how they organised the departure of non-Serbs from Kamengrad, Muslinovci [phoen], Sanski Most, Pobrijezje, and so on. All of these were organised convoys. People got into these vehicles. Some people were taken across Travnik, Vlasic, and so on. Others went a different route, who knows where. But what usually happened was that the people who were captured and detained, their families weren't able to leave. Hand-grenades were thrown at them, they were threatened over the phone, and so on. And then you had to ask the Serb authorities for a permit to take your children out alive and your family out alive. So she couldn't leave, and I assume the reason was because I was in detention. So they wanted to keep my family there so that they could do to them what they did to other families, which is to kill them. They would certainly have killed my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, whether families were killed and what happened. But you said two things there, there were two points you made. First of all, you said that your wife did not have the connections she needed to allow her to board the buses and leave, and you said that all those who had no connections had no chance of getting on to the buses. So how could somebody who was being expelled wouldn't have a place in a bus to leave? Mr. Zulic, they weren't expelled. It was them forcing the authorities to allow them to leave; that's the conclusion one can draw from what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the conclusion you can draw from what I said. You're telling us what you want people to hear. I'm telling you the truth, and I think in my statement somewhere it says that in Pobrijezje we were told for the first time that we would be moving out, and then we were told, You're not going now, you're going next time, while they were picking up the refugees for Kladusa and so on. First of all, Jajce, then they returned them, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only were they not expelled, but they -- the Serb authorities would tell them when the convoys would be organised so that they could prepare themselves. For example, the village of Husinovci or Pobrijezje, and then a selection would be made in those villages and they would say, Right, her husband is in the camp at Manjaca or at the camp in Betonirka, so she can't board the bus or truck or whatever. That's what they would do. In the best of cases it was buses, otherwise it was freight trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they would make this announcement over the radio, is that right, that there'd be a convoy for such and such a village; is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then they allowed some people to get into the buses and others not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second point that we have to address here and throw light on is this: You mention all the very small differences between you and your brothers, but a major difference strikes the eye. Your brothers did not have a machine-gun and they did not have explosives, otherwise everything was the same, they were Muslims, they were citizens of Sanski Most. The only difference between you and them, although they were from the same mother and the same father, is that they didn't have a machine-gun and explosives and you did?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say I didn't have any explosives, so don't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we're going to prove that and show that during these procedures.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can do what you like, but I know this man Djoko very well, but I'm telling you now I didn't have any explosives. Had I had explosives I would have said so straight away, Your Honours, just as I acknowledged having a machine-gun. That's why I'm here, to say what happened. Furthermore, my brothers, had they not left, they would have ended up where these others ended up, the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it because in Pobrijezje, 42 men remained until the end of the war. And my youngest brother, the one working in the mine, purely by chance, stayed alive. Arkan killed all the rest in the village of Sasin [phoen] in 1995, 64 men, able-bodied men were killed, and after the liberation of Sanski Most about 300 to 400 women and children were found in Sanski Most and ten Serbs, according to my knowledge and information. Whether that's the right figure or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, if you introduce new elements into your testimony all the time, then all this is going to last much longer and I'm going to have to ask the Trial Chamber for you to come back for another cross-examination because if you say that somebody from the Serb army, whether they be a volunteer or whatever but under the united command of the Serb army, could kill some civilians in cold blood, I have to throw light on that case. So please stick to your statement, otherwise we'll never get to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Concentrate on your examination. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the only difference was not the explosives and the machine-gun, just the machine-gun you say. Now, how come you make the conclusion that your two brothers would have been killed had they not left Sanski Most, whereas third brother worked in the mine in 1995, almost until the end? That means he had to go from his home to the mine every day to work in the mine, and then go back home from the mine and nobody killed him. So how can you then make the conclusion that your other two brothers would have been killed had they stayed on in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even if this youngest brother wasn't an expert, they wouldn't have kept him there. So it was just through force of chance that he stayed alive because in April his children, in 1995 -- well, they hid him. His two daughters hid him when Arkan was going through the village searching for men. So the fact that he wasn't killed is because they needed him to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they didn't need you to work? You were an expert too, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Serbs were up at the front, they needed every man they could get?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't need me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see, that's why they let you go and arrested you, not because you had a machine-gun; is that it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they let everyone go -- they dismissed all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about your brother?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was let go too, and then they introduced these labour obligations. It was called a work obligation that you were under.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish. I'm waiting for the interpreters to do their work, but I'll carry on. I have to finish what I was saying. So there was this work obligation, and everybody had to report to dig trenches and to do what the Serb fighters needed, to chop wood and so on. This is what I learned after the war. Let me make that clear. This is what I learned after the war. So that these people were usually escorted, under escort from Serb soldiers and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I'm afraid we're not going to get through this cross-examination even in a week's time, so I have to clarify the situation. Your brother, was he taken from home to the mine under police escort or could he go alone?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never went to work alone, on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other Serbs went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean his Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But was he under police or military escort or a police patrol taking him from home to work and back again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that there was always a Serb who went to work with him and came back from work with him. That's what I know, the Serb was some sort of official. I don't know what he was. But that's what he told me, that's the story he told me, so I'm telling you it now, what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned Mr. Simo Simetic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned in that context a policeman who helped the Muslims, and his name -- what was his name Milan Tontic or Tonci?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as Tonci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you recognise him if you were shown a photograph of him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might if it was an early photograph taken during that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a photograph of the man? 1D27, could that be placed on our screens, please. Your Excellency, there is a bit of a doubt whether it's available because some documents were left out of e-court by technical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's here. Let's check whether it's [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the man?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't identify him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't recognise him. He looks much older.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But does it look like the man?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. He -- his hair was totally different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then 1D24. 1D24 is a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, you confirmed yesterday that Tonci was alive, whereas in your statement you said that Serbs had killed him -- sorry, in one testimony you said he was killed by the Serbs because he had helped the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that I heard he was killed. I didn't confirm it. I don't know whether the man is alive or not. I cannot confirm. When I say I heard he was killed, that means I heard. If you say he's alive, then thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 of your amalgamated statement, 718, paragraph 63, as well as in your testimony in the Milosevic trial, transcript 6972, it says Serb policeman Tonci helped the Muslims and he was the only one he didn't beat them, that's why Tonci is no longer alive today. That's a statement, a claim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the information I had, and on that basis, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We now have 1D24, and this is a document that confirms that Tonci is still alive today, and this is an excerpt from the civilian register from Banja Luka from which it is obvious he's alive and he lives there.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only too happy if he's alive. I just told you that I was told after the war that he had been killed. I had no information to the contrary. If I knew the man was alive, I would have visited him, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, don't take it against me. I'm just saying that you are too loose with your statements. You claim things you can't know about. Your statement says something quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The name the witness referred to in his statement was -- the name of the Serb policeman was Tonci, but the name of this gentleman whose picture is before us is Tontic, as I read it. What's the basis on your part that the two are the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Tonci is a nickname, not a surname. In our parts, nicknames are usually formed on the basis of the last name or its shortened version. All of us, almost, have nicknames and they are based usually on the last name, not the first name. There was no other policeman with the surname beginning with "Ton."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, it was just an explanation for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zulic, I would like to put to you a couple of things that should not upset you. It's no accusation against you. I just want to hear from you: Yes, no, or I don't know. I don't have to go through all of this today, but we have to get to the facts. I will tell you how we see things and you will say: Yes, no, or I don't know. In the course of 1991, especially in the first half of 1991 and all the way up to May 1992, at the level of the republic and the level of municipalities there were negotiations about the transformation of Bosnia pending its recognition; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "transformation." Could you repeat that question or place it in a different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, the Serbs had accepted that the entire Bosnia should no longer be part of Yugoslavia, should separate, accepting the proposal of the European community that Bosnia would be transformed with three cantons, mainly ethnically determined, and that agreement was sanctioned in 1992. In parallel, there was a process of negotiations concerning the transformation of municipalities, and there were long talks for a long time successful in Sanski Most about forming two municipalities, one Serb, one Muslim. And these talks took quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know they were talking about something -- they were talking about something in the municipality, possibly about dividing it. It could have been on the 18th of March. I really can't remember the date and I cannot confirm the date. I know that these talks were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Serbs took power, took over in Sanski Most in 1990, and in 1992 they were strong and powerful in every respect. They held a greater part of the authorities than the Muslims, and the Serbs insisted that Muslims too form their own municipality in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they persisted or not, I don't know. I know there were negotiations about division. I know certainly about the division of the police force in Sanski Most. I believe I mentioned it in one of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we will look at the transcript from a session of the SDA board of Sanski Most, from which it will be evident that they were negotiating and what they were negotiating about. D1 -- sorry, 1D9 is the document I would like to call up. We have it on the screen now. This is a meeting held on the 16th March 1992. At that point in time in Sarajevo, there were intensive talks in Sarajevo that would end on the 18th of March, 1993, with the famous Lisbon Agreement, which means acceptance of the Cutileiro Plan. But let's go back to Sanski Most. Did I say 1993 or 1992? It should be 1992. The session was convened by the president of the SDA Sanski Most, Mr. Redzo Kurbegovic. Guests of the session are officials of the SDA Sanski Most, the secretary of the -- I'm being warned to slow down when reading. And from the centre in Sarajevo, there is a representative Osman Brka. Have you heard about him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a high official of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How high? A metre 80? 2 metres?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very witty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man, I only know that he was tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you know Redzo?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Redzo personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the agenda briefing about the current political and security situation in the territory of the republic and the operation of the SDA. Will you read this or --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this politics? I'm not going to read this. I didn't come here -- Your Honours, I've been saying for the umpteenth time that I'm not a politician. I never was involved in politics. If I know people, I'll say I know them. If I don't know some people, I'll say I don't know them. These politicians and what they were doing, I don't know. At that time we were only allowed to go to work and back home and listen to the radio a little. That's the only information I had. What was going on behind the scenes, all these things I have no idea about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this. Who restricted your freedom in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know at that time that president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Alija Izetbegovic; the foreign minister was a Muslim, Alija Delimustafic; and the minister of defence was Jerko Doko; the chief of police in Sanski Most was Burnic; the commander of the Territorial Defence was a Muslim, Halilovic. So who restricted your freedom in March? Yugoslavia still existed at that time. Bosnia is still part of Yugoslavia. Who restricted any of your freedoms in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which Serbs and how?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Easily. From January 1992 at all check-points - and it's in my statement, Your Honours - at all check-points there stood Serb soldiers wearing all sorts of uniforms. They asked you to produce your ID. If they saw you were a Muslim, they will search you and inspect you. If they see it is a Serb by the ID, they will let them go. That's how they searched cars and everything else. They would also ask you, Where are you going? If it's a private passenger car, they would send you back home. If it's a service car and you're going on business, they would let you go but say you have to come back in ten minutes exactly. And you really couldn't get to the other side. Whatever -- all these names that were just listed, I knew that Enver was the commander of the police; however, he had no say at that time. He didn't play a role. I don't see why he's asking me these things when I made it clear in my statement that it was already so at the beginning of January 1992. Mr. Karadzic only makes the point that Republika Srpska functioned in certain territories in full, and the 8th of March is still celebrated as the day of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to this statement, but I have to answer this. The Republika Srpska did not operate until the war broke out, and we will prove that. I just want you to be precise in your statement. Any expansion you make poses new challenges to me and makes it incumbent on me to ask additional questions. Let's look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please bear in your mind that you are not giving evidence. Just put the questions to the witness, and I note the time. Concentrate on real issues -- concentrate on your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I wasn't intending to make a problem of this again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 9 of your statement: [In English] "From April 1992, military police manned the check-points and there were no longer Muslims among them and if they stopped Serbs they wouldn't check them, they would just let them go but they would check the Muslims. They would check their cars. And that happened to me a few times." [Interpretation] The rest is redacted. Sir, only when the war broke out as of 6 April onwards, according to your statement, "there were no longer any mixed check-points," until the 6th of April, the patrols at check-points were assigned by Enver Burnic, and frequently there were more Muslims than Serbs in these crews, in these patrols; is that so?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not so because I know that only one Muslim was in Pobrijezje. From what I know there was only one Muslim from 1991. It was Hajro Oknic; only one Muslim at that check-point or whatever you call it. Were you in Sanski Most? Do you know better than I? Enes Burnic[as interpreted], you say he assigned people, Enes Burnic [as interpreted] had nothing to do with it. Nobody asked him a thing. Brane Sobot did all this. Now, after the war, everyone found out who made the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a procedural matter for the accused. The rest of that paragraph 9 has been redacted from the public version of the document. If he wishes to -- and as for this redaction and the other three redactions in the statement, if he wishes to take the accused [sic] to that, he would have to go into private session, but it's not redacted as evidence and Mr. Karadzic can do with it with the witness. It's redacted from 65 ter 90111A --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the document which is appearing on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm just saying if the accused wants to discuss matters that are redacted, he has to go into private session and we can go to the Exhibit P717. This is Exhibit P718 because it's the public version. I was just alerting the accused to that in case he thinks he can't deal with it because it's redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he understands. Thank you for your intervention. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Sutherland. But I don't need this because this passage does not relate to my subject. I wanted to avoid going into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to this meeting of the SDA on the 16th of March, 1993 -- sorry, 1992. I think it's quite clear that until April, and according to your statement that's true, there were mixed patrols. We'll leave the subject, unless you want to go on. Let's look at this meeting on page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2, 1D9. The previous document. The one before this one. Here we are. 1D9 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to read out a few excerpts. It says at the top: "Osman Brka," he says, "that everything that happened should have happened," and then he goes on to say: "I have to say that all this is necessary." And at the end of the paragraph, he goes on to say: "For the Muslim people which -- who are in full swing, the awakening of the Muslim people in full swing. It is important to be organised with Allah's help, and we will be the moral and overall winners to emerge from this chaos." And then further down he says, "there will be more victims and who knows what else, but in return we'll obtain what we want." Then towards the end of the page he says: "Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Ejup Ganic are doing their jobs very well, given the situation." Now may we have the next page, please. Next page. Next page. Yes, they're handling the situation well. A little further down for the Serbian version, please. The Serbian version. The Serbian version could you zoom down. That's fine. Mr. Brka says: "It's important to be well organised up until the time when it will become our legal army. We have to gain time and prolong matters?" And then Salim Sabic goes on to say: "I think that our people are very well organised. I think that when things come to a head, our people will be able to respond. We agreed to sign a statement to freeze all activities relating to the proclamation of the Serbian or Muslim municipality. They would not accept, under any circumstances, to remain in the Muslim canton. We don't have to trust the Serbs in anything." And then Sabic goes on to say -- it seems to be a new page, page 3. He proposes the following. Sabic again. Let's go on to page 3. Let's move on to page 3, please. It says -- what does it say here? Oh, these are the proposals, right: "Contact the police commander, the commander of the TO, ensure weapons for the units." As we know, the police commander was Mr. Enver Burnic, the man you say wasn't asked about anything, whereas they are giving him these tasks to carry out for the party. The commander of the Territorial Defence is Mr. Halilovic, also a Muslim. Now, Osman Djukanovic on that same page says: "The commander and I agreed that we should -- he said that we can count on self protection." Now, on -- we have it in English, and he says who's in charge of Vrhpolje, Tomina, Kijevo, and Capljina. It says "Haso and Emir." For Husinovci, the people in charge are commander P. Ibro, I don't know who that is. For Trnovo and Sehrevci -- it's difficult to read, but anyway, sir, what I want to put to you is this - you can say you don't know or you do know or you knew nothing about it - but on the 16th of March, the SDA is devising a variant to ensure that they are victors, emerge from the situation as victors, with the Lisbon Agreement and so on, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they discussed. I have to repeat again, Your Honours. I'm not a politician. I said that yesterday. I've been saying that all the time. I'm not a politician, and now putting it to me that way, I suppose that means that we Muslims should have just lay down and waited for them to slaughter us. Because in December 1991, around Sanski Most -- well, Sanski Most is in a valley, and the JNA had already taken up artillery positions around Sanski Most, which means, I assume, that they reacted to a situation like that. I don't know, but I assume. I don't know what they did, whether they did this, as it says here, who they reached an agreement with, I don't know. But I can say that Enver Burnic was the police commander and this other man Nijaz was the commander of the Territorial Defence. I know that Nijaz was disarmed on the 18th of April, 1992. I do know that. And Enver Burnic, he was disarmed on the 18th of April, 1992. That I do know because they worked in Betonirka together with me. So that's how I come to know that. Now, what they agreed about over there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, how far is Croatia from Sanski Most, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, well, I don't really know. When I fly by plane, they don't say. When I drive, it's about 90 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean going doing down the Sana River valley, Bosanski Novi to Dvor, that way?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I usually take the Kostajnica route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this other route is quicker, right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you know that at that time, the JNA was waging war in Croatia and that Sanski Most and Bosanska Krajina was the first territory in its rear?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Enver Burnic, the person you mentioned, was he a member of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know because I wasn't a member of any league, and that's what I'm trying to tell you. I did not belong to any of those political or whatever --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. I'm not claiming that. Tell me this: Did the Patriotic League have a branch in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If it did, it did; if it did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the decision to form the Patriotic League was taken on the 31st of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I'm hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are you hearing that the Patriotic League existed for the first time now?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the existence of the Patriotic League after the war, when I returned home, that's when I heard about the Patriotic League and its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have called up a document -- a Defence document, 1D11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After this we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the document on our screens now. This document was issued by the municipal court of Sanski Most in 1997, on the 14th of July. That is to say when Sanski Most was in the Federation because these are the Muslim authorities that we're talking about here; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't want to read it all. You have it in front of him, but Burnic, Enver, son of Mustafa and Fatima, has been declared dead; is that right? And Burnic, Hadzira, has submitted a proposal to this court that a judgement be pronounced to proclaim her husband dead. According to what she says, after the aggression against BiH, her husband who, as before, was the commander of the police in Sanski Most was prominent in the defence of the country -- yes, I'm being asked to slow down but I do believe that there's a translation there. Anyway, as commander, police commander in Sanski Most, he was prominent in the defence of the country. He refused to submit to the ultimatum of the SDA and be loyal to the Serb authorities, et cetera. It says the fascist SDS, so the -- they had already judged us fascists. Then it goes on to say witnesses who will testify stress that Burnic, Enver, was very patriotically oriented. And then in the middle of that paragraph it goes on to say that he worked actively to prepare an armed resistance to the aggressor, and on his uniform and cap he placed an insignia of the Patriotic League, or rather, the lily emblem. Is it clear to you that the Patriotic League existed, that it had its insignia, and that Enver Burnic placed that insignia on his cap as commander of the joint police force and with insignia like that walked around Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with -- are you asking whether I agree? How can I agree when I didn't see Enver wearing that kind of cap? I saw Enver in Betonirka; when I was taken there, I found him there and he was wearing slippers and some sort of shirt. So I don't know any of that. If somebody wrote that, it's not my problem and it's not up to me. I can't say anything about that. I can't make any comments. All I can say is what Enver looked like when I came across him. Now, did he wear a cap or hat, I don't know, he would have worn whatever he wanted on his head, horns or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 54 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we will take a break for 20 minutes. When we resume in 20 minutes, you will be given 30 minutes to conclude your cross-examination. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I hope I'm not going to have to ask the Trial Chamber for additional time or for you to come back another time. So if you were to give me yes or no answers, perhaps we could complete this on time. Did Enver Burnic, in Betonirka, while you were there, when you were detained, did he tell you anything about what this record speaks of?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in many villages around Sanski Most are there Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there fighting going on in those villages?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Vrhpolje, but in the rest no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there fighting in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no fighting in Hrustovo, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I see. Now I'm going to put my case to you and you can say yes or no. In Sanski Most, a large number of villages had a mixed population. Tomina was half/half Serbs Muslims, a 50/50 ratio, and in Tomina there was no fighting; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The mosque wasn't destroyed nor was anybody disturbed and they all lived together -- or rather, the Serbs still lived -- the Muslims still lived there; is that right, not the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the Muslims were expelled from Tomina in 1992. The mosque was destroyed in Tomina, so that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to show evidence about that. We have Zemina and her statement, and she talks about these things. Is it true and correct that the fighting, or rather, the conflict was around Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, four villages, Mahala, Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and which were the others? What was the other one? Just a moment, please. Can you tell us the villages where there were clashes?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to explain something here. There wasn't a conflict in Vrhpolje. From Vrhpolje upwards in that other place, they didn't clash there, the Territorial Defence and the paramilitary formations. They didn't clash in Vrhpolje or in Hrustovo, but there's another place above Vrhpolje which is where those groups were concentrated, the Muslim groups, putting up a resistance. But in Vrhpolje proper, in Hrustovo, in those villages, there was no fighting. I've just remembered. The place is called Galaja, it's about -- well, it's outside the village, further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulic. I'd like us to go back to the village of Hrustovo now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we have document 1D30 called up again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you turn on your microphone. Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. May we have page 3 of this document, please. No, it's not page 3. Well, yes, towards the bottom of page 3 it says: "Parallel to the increasingly prominent presence of regular units of the former JNA." And we agreed that the JNA existed until the 19th of May, right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's general knowledge, it's a generally known fact: "At the initiative of some individuals in the party of democratic action, the gathering of weapons and the formation of smaller assault units under the supervision of the organisation of Bosna Green Berets began. One such group operated in the town itself and very quickly groups were organised in Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Hrustovo, and parts of Kamengrad."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have page 5 displayed, please. We're looking at page 5 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page it says: "This meant the beginning of any and many attempts to take over the villages of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. At the same time, that is the period of frequent artillery activity against these villages from several positions held by the aggressor. The lines of defence of Vrhpolje unit were established by the Vrhpolje bridge and -- yes, by Vrhpolje bridge, and at that time, they were unattainable for the aggressor with a tactic of weakening the lines and frequent artillery attacks the enemy attempted daily to break down the resistance of the defenders. Besides a part of the unit that secured the Vrhpolje bridge, a part of the unit was stationed in the forests of Vrhpolje, Galaja, where the necessary conditions for life and training of the field unit were created."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have document 1D -- or rather, before we go on to that, could you focus on page -- on paragraph 32 of your amalgamated statement where you say that the regular -- on the 27th of May, 1992, [In English] The regular army and the reservists gathered the population of Mahala in the soccer field located in Krkojevci. The population of Muhic was gathered in the driving school training and on the road to Kljuc," and so on, and so on." Further: "The population of Mahala was asked to leave their houses so that the Serbian forces could deal with the Green Berets. The same day I also heard on the radio that the Green Berets had attacked the Serbian forces in Hrustovo. That was simply not true." Now may we have 1D15, please, which is a list of the fallen Serb fighters, fighters who were killed in Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in Hrustovo, the persons that were killed were those listed under number -- from number 3 onwards, Cedo Lazic; number 4, Rajcic, Goran; 5, Vaso Stupar; 6, Mirko Cicic; 7, Rade Malic; 8, Marko Ljuboja; 9 Bogdan Rajic; 10, Milivoj Majkic; and 11, Milorad Panjak. So, sir, there was fighting in Hrustovo. There were 900 armed and organised fighters who had been prepared even before the outbreak of the war, yes or no or you don't know, but just without a discussion. I can accept all three answers.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't make me say yes or no and put words into my mouth. I have to explain what you're asking me about. Your Honours, I have to explain certain things because there's explicit mention of Hrustovo here, and in Hrustovo, according to my statement and everything else, says that there were units -- well, the report said -- what I mean is that the defence was at Vrhpoljski bridge and Galaja forest, so that's not Hrustovo nor is it Vrhpolje, so it's Galaja forest. Those are two different things. So who attacked there, I don't know. I'm wondering what the Serb forces were doing in exclusively Muslim villages, and the epilogue of all of this is 300 people were killed in Hrustovo, that was the upshot, and in Vrhpolje when the defence was routed. That's what I heard, but I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zulic, we saw in the book of Zilhad Kljucanin that from the moment when the Muslim military forces in Hrustovo decided to launch an offensive, it is at that moment that the Serb forces responded, not when they were just standing guard. We can look at the document again, but I'm wasting time. And I'm just referring to your paragraph 32 in your statement, where you say: "It is not correct that Serb forces were attacked and it's not correct that there was fighting there." Whereas I am putting it to you now that in the Sana Valley River which includes Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor Bosanski Novi, there was an elite unit of the Patriotic League which caused clashes beginning with the 23rd of May in Prijedor and on to the end of May. It was defeated. And your author, Mirza Mujadzic, president of the SDA of Prijedor, writes that it is still unclear today how an elite unit of the Patriotic League was defeated so quickly in Prijedor. I don't want you to debate. I want to see the status of your statement in this trial, your statement was used for a conviction in the Brdjanin and the Krajisnik trials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is to say I confirm, I deny, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't read this. I don't know any of this. I put in my statement what I know, what I heard from the refugees. And when I wrote the statement, I made it clear I heard it from the refugees, from Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, from those who managed to escape. And that's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 32, in your statement, you say: "This was simply not true."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is simply not true. I don't know what you mean to say by calling them an elite unit. How many men were they? An elite unit can number 10 or a hundred men or 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about your paragraph 32, it ends with the words: "This was simply not true."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Mr. Zulic, since we don't have enough time, we have to deal with certain things that must be clarified and that includes the incident at Kriva Cesta. This is what you say about it, and I maintain that you made up the whole event, and you said that there was a huge commission for slaughter, including the president of the municipality, Rasula, who you didn't see with your own eyes but you heard his voice through the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you identified him only by his voice?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By his voice and his suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see his face?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say General Milan Daljevic was there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the well-known general from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was from the Second World War or not, I don't know. I know where he comes from and when he came to Sanski Most, and I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that there were many people sitting there and there was even a lot of Serbian elite looking and enjoying watching Celo slaughtering Muslims, and there was Milan Daljevic and Rasula among them whose political ideas I don't share and who viewed the SDS as critically as the SDA. Was Milan Daljevic there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you show me that paragraph where I said that Milan Daljevic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, here is your statement. It's in your statement paragraph -- I'll let you know which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's paragraph 79, to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 79, sir. Answer, please. Was Milan Daljevic there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All these Serbs you enumerated which are more numerous even than those who were slaughtered, were they on this panel that watched people being slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this Simetic really cut the throats of 20 people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some he did. Maybe he -- some others killed the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What will you say if Simo Simetic was in the corridor at that time, in his unit. He was not a policeman, he was a soldier. What will you say if I tell you that we have proof and that he will personally sue you for libel and perjury because he has proved that he was in his unit at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can get any certificate he wants. Even I can get, for money, any certificate for anything. Your Honours, I have a scar given me by Simo Simetic, here, right here, you can see it from the knife, his knife, and here I have a cross carved on my skin. You can see the cross carved on my chest. I would like him really to sue me. I can't wait for his trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have document 1D32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, are you okay? We can go on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1D32.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a state authority municipality of Prijedor, chief of the administrative service, the section for invalids of war. It's not translated. I'll read it: "Certificate that Simo Simetic," and then his unique citizen's number, "permanently residing in Prijedor," at such and such a street, "was a member of the armed forces of the SFRY, Republika Srpska, for the duration of the state of immediate threat of war, namely from the 17th of August, 1991, until 10 December 1996, military post 7421 Sanski Most, and from 11 December 1996 to 10 April 1996, he was in a different military post in Prijedor." How come, Mr. Zulic, that such a dramatic event attended by the political and every other elite headed by a national hero who's critical of the SDS, how come that nobody mentions it, nobody was tried, and the event is totally unknown?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That nobody was tried, and there is another piece of evidence in the Office of the Prosecutor about this man, I don't know why you haven't received it. If this certificate is important, I don't know how he got it. He wasn't in Prijedor, he was in Sanski Most. He came almost every night along with Danilusko Kajtez. They came almost every night to beat us in Betonirka. There is proof of that as well, and there is another piece of evidence, the post mortem of a Muslim man who was found in 1995 or 1996, I don't know. It coincides completely with all that I have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Except that he wasn't slaughtered by having his throat cut. He was shot by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the post mortem report says, and I had this report in my hands, it says that the body is in a good state.
