And I would kindly ask the Office of the Prosecutor to present this document here, including the post mortem report produced by the doctor in Sanski Most, Ibro Eminic, and that his son's statement be read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read now what we have: "Concerning the event on or around the 22nd June near the partisan cemetery, this event is completely invented, in which Simo Simetic is prepared to give evidence, a butcher from Sanski Most, alleged butcher, also two other eye-witnesses are prepared to give evidence. The only truth is that on this location" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused slow down when reading, please, this cannot be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it from the witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We got this from our investigators, and it says the post mortem says that both victims were shot from fire-arms, and they were found in two different ends of Sanski Most, and there was no other trace on the road of any slaughtering or massacre. There was and there is no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask the Prosecution to read the post mortem report by the doctor. What Mr. Karadzic is saying is a report from some people who are all unidentified perpetrators. All of them were allegedly killed in different locations. In my statement, I said that it was impossible to bury anyone because it was a brook, a river. All these reports are doctored.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll find evidence of that elsewhere at another time. You say that Serbs announced where there will be bombing, that they rounded up civilians from Mahala at the stadium and said they needed to deal with the Green Berets, both in Mahala and in Vrhpolje and in Hrustovo, and that, among other people, your mother-in-law was also called up on the radio. It was all announced on the radio and the civilians were invited to gather in one place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, how much more time do I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you finish in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you were transported by lorry. How many of you were there in the lorry, 60?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what position were you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sitting down, standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could 60 people sit down in such a truck?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said both sitting down or standing up. Some people who got in first sat down, others stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could some people sit down when it is hardly possible for 60 of them to stand? There's just no room enough.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when we really had to do it, we had to ask each other to -- for one to spread the legs so the other one could press himself against him. They were just pushing us in with sticks and cables and truncheons. We were being packed in and I know exactly how, without water, without anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that situation, let's just leave it at that. Sixty people, if there were 60 people, they all had to be standing. And still, you had enough room to take this small bottle and urinate into it and drink that urine. How did you manage?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply, very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have to bring such a bottle once here and try it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be done now if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, you said you had your own block at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was Dr. Dervis Kadic there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they found a needle on one prisoner?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come they didn't find your notepad?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, let me clarify about the notepad. I received it sometime in August from a Serb, and in that notepad there were telephone numbers, if I ever get out of there alive so I can call my family in Germany and abroad. And I kept -- I buried it first into the ground, this notepad, and then I urinated on it. And then they would always say, God, fuck his mother, he's pissing below him, under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that in any statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but now you're asking me how I managed. I'm trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The other three or four notebooks you wrote somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In camp when I left Karlovac -- in Cologne when I left Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So is that a diary or your memoirs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my memoirs copied out from the notepad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just copied out the names from your notepad?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then I wrote according to my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they were your recollections and not a diary where entries were made as the events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I didn't make the entries as the events took place, but when I went to Cologne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did your military service in the navy in Split; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us here that your disability resulted from the beatings you received at Manjaca or Betonirka; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why in the army were you listed as unfit?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had an ulcer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it says, but it said ulcus duodenum in my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have called up on e-court document number 1D, Defence document -- I have it here. Just let me check the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to call up 22?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is, yes. Thank you, Your Excellency. 1D22. That's the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under number 608, on this document, it says Ahmet Zulic, son of Azem, or rather, Aziz, and in the last column, it says "unfit, cessation of military service," on such and such a date. So you went to do your military service and they found you to be unfit for service but there's no diagnosis, the one you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. They just failed to write it in. I know why. They said they couldn't provide the kind of food that I needed with an ulcer and that they didn't have the necessary medicaments, so that's why they wrote this "unfit," Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1967 or 1966. I can't be quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zulic, you agree that this is an entry which is related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree that that is me. I'm just telling you the diagnosis for which I was released from the army. It was a duodenum ulcer, the diagnosis was in Latin, but translated into Bosnian is ulcer of the duodenum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think you managed very well since 40 years has passed. Do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have a lot of questions because his statement was a long one, but I don't want to broach new topics. Although, if necessary, I should like to ask to have this witness re-called at some point; otherwise, this completes my cross-examination at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you -- I take it you have some re-examination or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, this morning at page 43 of the LiveNote transcript, Mr. Karadzic was cross-examining you about the killings in Kriva Cesta, and he said that you identified Rasula being present there by his voice and his suit and that you didn't see his face. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said yesterday in your transcript at page 33 of the yesterday's LiveNote that you had known Rasula for well over 30 years. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have to see his face or what he was wearing, although he was always in a dog's-tooth jacket with a red tie and had the kind of hair that he had. So I didn't need to see his face. Just hearing his voice I would be able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that he was always wearing this particular suit. What is the name for this particular suit in B/C/S, in your language?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called it "pepita," which is the black-and-white little squares, chequered like little rhomboid shapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said he was always wearing this jacket.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. A whole suit actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were also asked just a moment ago about the disabilities as a result of the injuries, your disabilities. What disability -- what injuries did you suffer permanently as a result of the beatings that you incurred in Betonirka and Manjaca and the end -- what occurred to you at the incident at Kriva Cesta?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I think I said, and it says in my statement, that six -- seven of my vertebrae have been damaged, that all my ribs were fractured, and I showed you the scars earlier on, and that this finger was broken because they stepped on that one because they wanted the three fingers to remain to make the sign that I told you about when I was doing push-ups. And you can see that this finger was fractured. And in addition to that - and I have nightmares about this -- well, I have nightmares very often. I very frequently dream of people who were killed beside me or were dying beside me, so nightmares, generally. And I had one last night, but that, of course, is my problem, my personal problem, and it's something I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As a result of when you were at Kriva Cesta, was a gun placed into your mouth?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was taken to Kriva Cesta twice. I was taken to Kriva Cesta twice. The first time they took me away from home, and the second time when I was with this group of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, do you have -- do you have false teeth?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they pulled the gun out of my mouth, they bashed my teeth in wit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this was at the Kriva Cesta incident on the 22nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were asked questions about Simo Simetic. How often -- how -- how long had you known him for before you saw him on the 22nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the beginning of the war, as a butcher in Sanski Most, so a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war as a butcher?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I've just said. I've known him for ten years -- I knew him for ten years before the war. And Simo Simetic -- the whole town of Sanski Most knew that he was a little mentally disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Zulic. Again, on behalf of the Tribunal and the Chamber, I deeply appreciate your assistance and contribution to the Tribunal. Thank you for your coming all the way to The Hague to give your evidence. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we hear the evidence of the next witness, we need to deal with the exhibits of the Defence and also -- first of all, I have to check whether you are minded to tender any documents you used with this witness, Mr. Karadzic. Then we'll come to it. But before that, I need to -- I need to give some more guidance to the Prosecution on the process by which exhibits should be tendered in light of the experience yesterday with Mr. Zulic. Because it was the first witness, we just let it go, but this new -- this regime should apply to the Defence as well. For the Rule 92 ter witnesses, once the formalities of the admission of the 92 ter statement or prior testimony is completed, I would like the Prosecution immediately to tender that statement or transcript into evidence, as Ms. Sutherland did yesterday. Then the Prosecution should proceed to read out the short summary of the admitted statement or transcript. After reading that summary, the Prosecution should put its question to the witness. During such questioning, any of the associate exhibits listed in the Rule 92 ter notification may be put to the witness as may other documents, as happened yesterday. Immediately following this discussion with the witness of particular items, the Prosecution is required to tender that item into evidence, and the Chamber will then hear any objection from the Karadzic and proceed to rule on its admission. But otherwise, admission will be decided item per item when used -- directly used during the course of examination. At the end of the examination, if there remain any associate exhibits which have not been discussed with the witness and tendered into evidence, the Prosecution will be given the opportunity to tender those items and the Chamber will hear from the accused before ruling on their admission. I think this is more coherent and efficient manner in which to proceed rather than having the Prosecution tender the associate exhibits before it has put any questions to the witness, as occurred yesterday. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- with this witness, though, that all the documents that are associated with his statement are admitted because I didn't deal with every exhibit simply for that reason, because they were already admitted because they formed part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you are going to use it during the course of the examination, it's better for various purposes to be admitted during the course of examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but those documents that I didn't show he Mr. Zulic yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, those are -- they can be admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- at the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That regime should apply to you, Mr. Karadzic, as well. So if you are minded to tender the documents into evidence, in addition to using them during the course of cross-examination, you should apply so to the Chamber, and the Chamber will rule on its admissibility. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, you asked if there were any questions about the procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and I just wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- one point of clarification. If I understand this process accurately as the Court has described it, it's not necessarily an invitation to re-visit documents that were discussed extensively in the 92 ter statement; but instead it gives the Court an opportunity to be apprised of the full extent to which any particular document may have been discussed at the conclusion of all the evidence, both the 92 ter evidence and the evidence adduced in court. That's essentially the purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's entirely in your discretion whether to put any of the documents to the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic, I have the list of your exhibits to be used in relation to the previous witness, amongst which you used number 8, 9, 10, 11, 15, 22, 24, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32. Among them, what are you minded to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, thank you. To facilitate and expedite matters, I would kindly request that all these documents which were put to the witness be admitted into evidence. I'd like to tender them. And if I've understood you correctly, the opportunities and possibilities open to the other side to tender documents not shown, then I should like to put forward all the documents that we have, from 1 to 32, if that is possible. I'd like to tender them and have them admitted, but they'll always be confirmed and brought up again because they're usually state organ documents which we did not have time to go through but which relate to the testimony of the witness. So although he didn't comment on them, they are all documents with facts and contents, material facts which relate to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any observations on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would object to all of the documents that he's downloaded into -- uploaded into e-court for this witness to be tendered and only those documents that were shown to the witness, we can deal with those documents and those are the documents that you read out, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So in relation to document number 9, we would ask that that be MFI'd at this stage until we can review the full document because the document is -- there was only a partial translation, a summary translation of that document available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to check whether he has used 8 or not. Probably it's my mistake. He didn't use it. Yes. I was told that he used it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger will deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm only -- and I actually don't want to deal with the particular documents, but because this is the first time we're addressing many of these issues which will have larger- and longer-term implications, I wanted to make a few observations and clarify a few of the Court's guiding principles and some of the Prosecution's observations as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are allowing some latitude to the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Of course it's the Prosecution's position that the Court should get as much useful, relevant information as possible in order to make its decision. We appreciate at the same time there has to be some balance struck and the Court has to make a determination about where the line is drawn so it's not inundated with information. As a general matter, we do want the Court to get information. Now, with respect to a number of these documents, I note they were put to the witness, the witness had no knowledge about those documents at all. Therefore, the submission or the tendering of these documents for admission into evidence is, in effect, a bar table submission. Now, we don't -- we obviously don't discourage the bar table process, provided that the documents are both relevant and probative and reliable and those factors are clearly identified. But they need to be identified in that manner. In this case, in drawing or attempting to -- or in these instances I should mention, in attempting to strike the balance between the desire to get as much useful information as possible and the need to draw the line somewhere, the Court will have to make various assessments. But I note that many of these documents are not as probative or, at least, would not be given as much weight as many of the documents the Prosecution submitted in its recent bar table submission as official records, for example, or temporaneous recordings by participants in the various events at issue. So I don't draw any kind of rigid line, but I note that some of these would fall on the periphery, and the Prosecution notes that. In addition, there are quite a number of documents for which we haven't received a partial -- any translation at all or for which there are partial translations. Clearly, I think the Prosecution should have an opportunity to review those documents to determine whether other portions of the documents should be or may be proffered for admission to provide appropriate context, to corroborate testimony that was attacked by the same document, and so on. Some of those documents may, therefore, need to be marked for identification rather than have any particular decision made at the moment. So I wanted to make those preliminary observations because I think they will guide the process. We are tendering documents, both the Prosecution and the Defence. We're going to have -- we will be devising guide-lines and appropriate tests for such documents and we know there won't be a bright-line test in very many instances for certain categories of documents that's going to depend on those various factors. We want to ensure that the Court has all the information it needs to make this decision and is properly informed about the evidence it bears on these issues. To some extent, that's going to be a case-by-case determination. I think some of the factors I've outlined in this case will apply to all the documents, but in assessing the individual documents the accused has tendered for admission here I think those are a couple of factors we need to bear in mind. Finally, with respect to the documents the Defence didn't use, clearly if he's going to make bar table submissions about that, he needs to follow the appropriate procedure, and that is to identify, at a minimum, the relevance and providence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have further specific comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I meant Mr. Tieger was going to deal with the broader issue of documents, not that particular document. In relation to 1D10, we would ask that it be MFI'd at this stage. In relation to 1D11, we would also ask that it be MFI'd at this stage until we receive a full translation. In relation to document 1D15, we have no objection to that. I would note that that's part of one of our 65 ter numbers 17757. In relation to 1D22, we have no objection to that. In relation to 1D27, we do object to that and 1D29. In relation to 1D27, for the reasons that we don't know that this -- that the witness couldn't recognise this person. We don't know if this is, in fact, the person because the witness only knew of him by a nickname. We don't know whether, in fact, this is the right person. In relation to 1D29, we object to statements being admitted circumventing Rule 92 bis procedure or the witness being called to testify. In relation to 1D30 and 1D31, which are excerpts from an approximate 400-page document, we would ask that that be MFI'd until we can review that and put it into context, the pages that have been uploaded. And in relation to 1D32, we would ask that that be MFI'd until we receive an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, before you make a decision, I would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? First of all, we see now clearly what kind of difficulty the Defence is facing. If a witness is brought here together with a statement that is admitted a priori, a statement of 159 paragraphs, each of which is a piece of evidence, then the Defence would either need a lot more time for preparation and a lot more time for cross-examination to challenge and counter all these paragraphs. And if this is the position of Mrs. Sutherland, I am between a rock and a hard place, between restricted time for cross-examination and a one-sided approach to which we are not used. If we had an investigating judge here, or if the Prosecution had done their job in an unbiassed way and under the Rule 68 provided all the evidence, then we wouldn't have this problem. Now we do have a problem. The Defence has to do their job, or rather, the job of the investigating judge from our system. On top of that, I cannot understand that my 32 documents, including some that I didn't have time to show to the witness but that speak explicitly to the paragraphs from his statement, I cannot understand that they cannot be admitted. Then it means that I really have to have much more time for examination. Third, the example of Defence document number 8, it was seized by the UNPROFOR or the NATO when they were searching various locations in Republika Srpska, and here they seized a report of an operative officer which has no political or propaganda or media connotation. He simply reports to his centre about operative intelligence that is directly relevant to statements made by this witness in his written statement. What are we going to admit if we are not going to admit number 8, a document that the Prosecution disclosed to us and that they received after the searches conducted by NATO on the ground? As for number 29, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I don't want to interrupt your flow --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt, I'm sorry. I didn't deal with 1D008. We don't object to the admission of that document, and, in fact, it's 65 ter 20943. And I apologise for not dealing with that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I was about to say, Dr. Karadzic, this isn't the only opportunity that you're going to have to tender these documents into evidence. They can -- any document can be tendered into evidence during the course of the Defence case as long as its provenance and relevance is shown. So the fact that they're not being admitted at this stage is not a preclusion to them being admitted in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have more to say, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Thank you, Your Excellency. Just regarding what you just said, unfortunately among the accused and in our parts in the Balkans, the rule of thumb is that what you have done in the Prosecution case is the only thing that's done and not much attention is going to be paid to the Defence case. But I would like to draw your attention to the witness statement of Djordje Todorovic. This witness confirmed a few things from that statement. Yes, this is correct, this is correct, but I didn't take the exclusive. Everything else is confirmed, that his brother was working until the end of 1995 almost, et cetera. That's why I believe this statement is important. Generally speaking, I believe all these should be admitted or I should be given more time to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, one more broad point I think is clear that I think should prevail during the course of the proceedings, and that is that to the 92 bis process and procedure must prevail for the tendering of statements, and merely putting one's case to a witness that arises from a statement doesn't render that particular statement admissible in the absence of fulfilment of 92 bis or the appearance of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will have a break now for 30 minutes, after which we will rule -- the Chamber will give its ruling on this -- on the admissibility of these documents and hear the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. You had asked that each of us should introduce any fresh face that appeared in the courtroom, and I should just say that I'm accompanied, therefore, today by Ms. Mirjana Vukajlovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Welcome, Madam Vukajlovic. And I take it Mr. Tieger has a member to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Gaynor, Mr. Fergal Gaynor will be taking the next witness. And I believe he's known to the Court, but I introduce him formally in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Mr. Gaynor. We will give the ruling on the admissibility of the documents used by the Defence during his cross-examination of Mr. Zulic. Items, I just referred to the numbers. Numbers 8, 15, and 22 are admitted. Among them, number 8 and number 15 are not confirmed by the witness; however, considering the -- those exhibits were not contended or objected to by the Prosecution, we are admitting them. There are other documents number 9, 10, 11, 24, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32 are not admitted. The reason is as follows: The witness didn't confirm their content at all, nor did he give any evidence relating to the authenticity or foundation of those documents. In particular, Mr. Karadzic, regarding the statement of a witness or anybody else, we cannot admit it -- admit them in a vacuum. As Mr. Tieger properly indicated, we have a proper rule pursuant to which we can admit such documents. So you can have ample opportunity to use 92 bis, 92 ter regime later on. And as for the photograph, since the witness didn't identify the person in the photo, it has no probative value at all. And as to the book as well, the -- not only because the witness didn't confirm its content but also relevant parts are already put to the witness, there's no need to admit them all. Although the Prosecution suggested marking it -- marking them for identification and requesting for their translation, the Chamber is of the view that -- is of the view that since it should not be admitted, it does not need to be translated at all. But our decision, Mr. Karadzic, does not necessarily mean that you can't tender them into evidence through other witnesses, either by the course of cross-examination or during the course of Defence case. One point I'd like to make in this regard is that if the witness is not agreeing to or confirming the contents of these specific documents, you don't have to go over and over again as to its contents. I think it's clear from the advice of Judge Morrison of yesterday. There's one further matter, Mr. Tieger or Ms. Sutherland. It's about the 92 ter amalgamated statement of Mr. Zulic. My understanding is there are two kinds of -- two versions, one confidential, one redacted public version, and the reason why we have the public redacted version is that part of his amalgamated statement is -- was based on his evidence given in private session in previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But given the prior protective measures have been rescinded by the Court decision and the -- if the reason for giving evidence in private session in previous trial was because of the protection of his identity himself, then I don't think there's further need to retain the confidentiality of that part. So if you could come back to us with the reason -- what the reason was why he -- those -- evidence was given in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need to go to private session, you can request so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were four portions. The first portion, if I can take you to P717, and this shouldn't be broadcast on the screen. Paragraph 9, the last four sentences were redacted because that was dealt with in private session in the Krajisnik case. And on a reading of the transcript it would seem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have it before us, but -- Ah, yes, I have an unredacted version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is material that I don't -- it was dealt with in private session, and, therefore, that was why I redacted it from the statement, but on reading of the transcript it seems that it was something that was said in private session simply because they, the Court, had forgotten to go out of private session and back into open session. So it's something that doesn't -- wouldn't have identified the witness, but simply because it was dealt with in private session I redacted it. But I don't know it's something that needs to remain in private session for that reason, but we didn't have a decision -- we don't have a decision from that Trial Chamber and so we have to, as a matter of course, redact those things that are dealt with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but the reason they went into the private session was protection of Mr. Zulic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, his identity. And then they didn't come out of private session when they were dealing with this particular matter that's dealt with in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So I don't have any issue with that. In relation to paragraph 70, this was specifically dealt with when the witness was in open session and he actually asked to go into private session because he didn't want to say these -- what's contained in paragraph 70 in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He also stated today as well that if he wanted to say that he would go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, he said that yesterday. So I would ask that that still remain redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to paragraph 80, the fourth and fifth sentences, again that was actually in open session in Krajisnik but was subsequently redacted pursuant to an order of the Presiding Judge because it would identify him. And the same for paragraph 84, the second sentence in paragraph 84 -- no, I'm sorry, that was dealt with in private session. But the same thing, for those two reasons because it may identify him. And I don't think there's a problem at all with those paragraph 80 and 84 not being redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will give its guidance later on, after deliberating on this. And there's one further housekeeping matter. Ms. Sutherland, I remember the Chamber did not admit the 65 ter number 22038, list of persons arrested and detained because we haven't heard any evidence as to its authenticity or foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I failed to rule on its -- your motion to add it to the 65 ter list. So I didn't mean to exclude your possibility to introduce -- to tender that evidence through another witness. So your motion to add that item to the 65 ter list is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I was actually going to clarify that with you at the end of the -- your ruling this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That said, let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise one matter quickly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Harvey and with Mr. Sladojevic at the break about the possibility of releasing for today Witness KDZ-064. They agreed. I don't know if Mr. Sladojevic had an opportunity to convey that to Mr. Karadzic, but it simply means that the third anticipated witness would be able to go home today rather than waiting around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's plausible to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- hear that evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, while we're waiting, if I could quickly raise one point of clarification about the documents. With respect to larger documents for which certain excerpts are translated and tendered, the Prosecution was not suggesting that the entirety of the document be submitted for full translation, but simply that an opportunity be given to the Prosecution to review the untranslated portions to see if portions, in addition, should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, while we're waiting, can I just make a few points? It appears to me that your decision regarding language, the Serbian language for my needs, applied to transcripts, that transcripts need not to be translated. As far as I remember, that did not apply to the basic statements, and if my understanding is correct, I would kindly ask that witness statements that formed the basis for 92 ter be made available to me in the Serbian language. And secondly, we had some technical problems today with the uploading of documents, problems that were beyond our control, but I hope that they will have been dealt with by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Before Mr. Gaynor asks you some questions, I have some orders, Mr. Crncalo, for you. On behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, I would like to thank you for coming here to give evidence in this trial. The Chamber appreciates that this is the third time you have travelled to The Hague to testify in this case, and we hope that you understand the reasons why we were unable to hear your testimony on those previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are aware that such repeated journeys on your part are not easy and that you have had to make personal arrangements to accommodate us. So I wish to express our gratitude to you for being willing to come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, it's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: My name is Sulejman Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the 1st of November, 2009, you signed an amalgamated witness statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I request that 65 ter number 90014 be brought up and that we go to page 16 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the screen in front of you, Mr. Crncalo, underneath the declaration, you see your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, in fact, you signed every page of this statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you want to correct one word in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could page 9 of the statement be brought up, please. Now, Your Honours, on the fourth line of paragraph 52 of the statement, the witness refers to young soldiers in Pale who "wore Chetnik armbands, ribbons, on their arms and on their heads." Mr. Crncalo wishes to change the word "Chetnik" in that sentence to the word "red."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Crncalo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If I may explain. There were no insignia on them. There were just ribbons tied on both upper arms and around the head, red bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, subject to that correction, do you confirm that the amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked under oath about those topics today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Certainly this is my statement and I stand behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, I would seek to have the amalgamated witness statement admitted into evidence, that's number 90014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's admitted. What would be the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I forgot to give the numbers to the Defence documents, three documents, that we admitted, 8, 15, 22. What would the numbers be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit numbers would be D5, 6, and 7, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I now propose to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. Mr. Crncalo is a Bosnian Muslim who was born, lived, and worked in Pale. In 1991 and early 1992, Mr. Crncalo noted increased public manifestations of Serb nationalism in Pale, the covert distribution of weapons to the local Serb population, and the mobilisation of his Serb coworkers. In response, the Muslim community felt threatened and started guarding their households. On the 3rd of March, 1992, the witness was arrested by policemen while guarding his house, taken to Pale police station, interrogated by police, including the chief of police, Malko Koroman, threatened with death, and beaten for three hours. Shortly thereafter, Malko Koroman issued a call over the television directed to all non-Serbs to surrender all weapons to the police. Serb paramilitaries conducted searches of Muslim houses. At the beginning of March 1992, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Pale was established. It controlled all municipal activities. It was headquartered at the police headquarters and consisted of SDS leaders, including the SDS president, the chief of police, and the municipality president. In mid-March 1992 the Serb authorities started a campaign to convince Muslims to leave the municipality. A Serb police officer and a paramilitary unit commander, Radomir Kojic, came to the witness's street to deliver a message to the Muslims that it was better to leave in peace and thereby avoid trouble later. In the second half of March, a Muslim delegation from the municipality, including Mr. Crncalo, met with Nikola Koljevic and the Pale chief of police, Malko Koroman. Koljevic told the delegation that local Serbs did not want Muslims living in Pale. Koroman informed the delegation, in Koljevic's presence, that he could no longer guarantee the Muslims' safety, as he could not control the Red Berets who had arrived in the municipality. Intimidation of the Muslim population by armed Serbs increased in April 1992. Check-points, ordered and controlled by the SDS Crisis Staff, and manned by paramilitaries and reserve soldiers, severely restricted movement of Muslims and cut them off from neighbouring Muslim communities. In May 1992, the Crisis Staff ordered that telephones belonging to Muslims be disconnected. In mid-May, the witness and his fellow non-Serb coworkers were dismissed from work. Also in May 1992, Mr. Crncalo saw three civilian transport trucks full of civilian Muslim men from Bratunac arrive in Pale escorted by Serb paramilitaries. The president of the municipality, Starcevic, directed that the Muslim men be taken to the cinema where they were detained. In May and June 1992, there was a buildup of regular and paramilitary Serb personnel in the municipality. There were also random arrests of Muslims, and in June and July several Muslim men were arrested in their homes by Serb paramilitaries and killed. In June 1992, after the killing of Serb soldiers near Zepa, Radovan Karadzic gave a speech to a crowd in front of the Dom Kultur in Pale. Mr. Crncalo was present for part of the speech, and he heard Karadzic say words to the effect that the best way to defend Serb houses was to attack Muslim houses. In late June and early July, the Serb authorities organised convoys to forcibly remove non-Serbs from Pale. A written notice put up in the witness's area instructed the Muslim population where and when to gather in order to be transported out of the municipality. The Muslims gathered at the designated location, were permitted to take with them only what they could carry, and were transported in convoys of buses under police escort to Sarajevo. The witness was obliged to fill in a contract agreeing to transfer ownership of his house to a Serb woman. He was also obliged to leave behind his car and the registration papers to his car. The witness and his family left Pale town in the third of three convoys. The three convoys consisted of 18 buses in total. Each bus could hold 90 to a hundred people and each bus was packed full with non-Serbs. Mr. Crncalo has been shown four documents, all of which were issued by Bosnian Serb authorities in July 1992. Two were issued by the SJB of the Bosnian Serb MUP in Pale, one by the Executive Committee of Pale municipality, and one by the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All four documents state that the movement of Muslims out of Pale municipality was voluntary. Mr. Crncalo says that he does not know of any Muslim or Croat who left Pale municipality voluntarily in July 1992. Mr. Crncalo learned, after his expulsion from Pale, that the three mosques in the Pale area were destroyed between July and September 1992. He also learned that several Muslims who refused to leave the Pale area in July 1992 were killed. The witness's convoy went to Sarajevo, where the witness and his family lived for over three and a half years. Living conditions in Sarajevo during the siege were difficult. There was no heating and no running water where they lived. Only urgent medical cases received professional medical attention, as doctors and other medical staff had too many cases of serious injury to deal with. Food was in short supply. When the Serbs cut off humanitarian supplies to Sarajevo, the witness and others were forced to eat what they could find, including boiled grass and boiled leaves. The difficulty of life generally was compounded by anguish caused by the sight of blood on the streets and corpses which had not been collected for burial. Shelling and sniping were a constant and terrifying feature of life. On several occasions, Mr. Crncalo was near civilians killed by snipers. During the over three and a half years that he spent in besieged Sarajevo, he lived in constant fear that he or members of his family would be killed due to shelling or sniping. When Mr. Crncalo left the house, he was never sure that he would ever return alive, nor was he ever sure that those he had left behind would be alive when he returned. On 28 August 1995, Mr. Crncalo's wife went to the Markale market-place, as she had heard a rumour that powdered milk would be on sale there. She was killed when the market-place was hit by shelling. Mr. Crncalo, his son, and daughter continued to live in Sarajevo until the siege ended. At no time during the siege did he, or any of his family, have an opportunity to leave Sarajevo. Your Honours, I now intend to ask the witness several questions which are limited to clarifying and highlighting particular aspects of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The first subject, Your Honours, concerns paragraphs 36 to 41, which is on page 7 of the amalgamated statement. There's no need for it to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I would like you to focus on a meeting which took place in May 1992. You were part of a Muslim delegation of about 15 people who attended a meeting with Nikola Koljevic and Malko Koroman in a coffee shop in Pale. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see Nikola Koljevic at that meeting yourself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Nikola Koljevic with my own eyes and I can explain why he came there. We asked the police chief to get a higher official from the government to come to explain to us or to give us assurances that we can continue living in Pale together with our Serb neighbours. Nikola Koljevic replied to me, It's no use that you want it because Serbs don't want to live together with Muslims. Then Mr. Koroman, chief of police for Pale municipality, probably supported or encouraged that statement, saying that he, as police chief, Malko Koroman, is no longer able to keep under control the Red Berets that had come from Knin, and they had come to do their work. And we saw very well what kind of work they did in Knin. In Knin and in Gospic, fire swallowed everything, everything that could be looted was looted, everything that could be killed was killed. And they had the intention probably to do the same in Pale. That's why Malko Koroman told us that he could no longer keep them under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you just tell the Court, why are you certain that the person who you said was Nikola Koljevic, why are you so sure that that was Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was not alone. All of us who were there had occasion, many times, to see Nikola Koljevic on television, and there was also Vucic, a member of the government of Republika Srpska. And when he was supposed to come to this meeting with us, one policeman, Novica Stanar suddenly disappeared, but he wasn't gone long. He came soon back with one policeman, Predrag, and they brought Nikola Koljevic. He was dressed in a green jacket. All of us present recognised him. There is no dilemma whether that was him or not. Everyone recognised him. That was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Koljevic distance himself in any way from the words spoken by Mr. Koroman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, he didn't distance himself from anything. A strong drink was served, I didn't see what exactly, and they stayed on after we left. I mean us, the people who came seeking assurances of safety if they continued to live in Pale. We left that cafe bar and they stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move, Your Honours, to paragraph 78, which is at the top of page 14 of the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you referred in your previous evidence to a speech by Radovan Karadzic in Pale in 1992, in June 1992. Do you recall your previously testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did not testify before. I just gave witness statements. I never testified in a courtroom before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you for the correction. That's absolutely right. Now, going to that speech by Karadzic, where were you standing when he was speaking?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I stood next to a lamp-post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And where was Karadzic standing at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Karadzic was standing in the middle of the crowd of people in mourning, people whose nearest and dearest were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was he using a microphone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did not see a microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How far from him were you standing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Roughly 15 to 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you just tell the Court the words that you heard Karadzic say during his address, for that portion of his address that you were present.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I can. Those were terrible words to our ears. He was saying to those present that every Muslim house had to be attacked because that's the way to defend Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the last subject I'd now like to move to the final paragraphs of the statement, the events of the 20th of August, 1995. These are at paragraphs 94 to 97 on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I have to ask you to focus on the events of the 28th of August, 1995. Where were you on that morning?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That morning I was at home together with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your wife left the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In the evening, we heard some rumours that at the market in Sarajevo there was powdered milk to be bought, and milk was very important at that time, especially for children. And my wife decided to go and get the milk. She left the house around 8.30, and we agreed that she shouldn't linger, that she should be back no later than 11, hoping that she would stick to that agreement. I began to worry when she didn't show up after 11.00. I went towards the market-place to look for her. Halfway there, I ran into some people and started talking to them. They asked me, Where are you going? And I said -- and then they said, There was a catastrophe there. A shell fell and there was a massacre. And I continued walking to the site of that massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you to describe for Their Honours the scene at the market-place when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I will. When I got to that place, or rather, a few steps before, I saw a great mess and commotion. There was blood all over the place, flowing in the streets, bits of human flesh scattered around, bits of clothing torn and scattered all over, shoes mostly torn -- torn off human feet. That fence that was put up there for people to be a little safer when passing through, it looked like it was painted red from the blood. A passer-by told me to go to the Kosevo Hospital if I'm missing someone. I was hoping that it would not be the worst. I checked -- I wanted to check the lists of wounded people. I didn't find her on that list. I asked a doctor, Well, what shall I do? My wife is not on the list of the wounded people. He said, Go to the morgue. And when I got there, I found my wife. She was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. Crncalo: What impact did your wife's death have on you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: First of all, great sorrow. Second, until then I had been trying to provide money and clothing and food for my children. After she died, I had to be both father and mother. I had never cooked before, but from that time on, I had to cook, I had to clean my children's clothes, prepare children for school, supervise them on the way from home to school and back. I was able to have some sort of talk with my son, but it was horribly difficult with my daughter. But I had to. I had no choice. I had to keep them with me. I had to tell them something so that they would listen to me and go on going to school --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: -- that they continue with school. Thank God they listened to me. They completed school and now they are both employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, that finishes the examination-in-chief. I would now request that six exhibits be admitted in evidence. These are the -- they form an integral part of the amalgamated statement, and in accordance with Your Honour's direction, I will read out the 65 ter numbers of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, since we have all the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go through that, Mr. Crncalo, are you okay now? If you so wish, we may have a break, a short break for you. How are you feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main part of the evidence I've already got through, I managed to get through that. So if you like, I can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any observation on the -- these documents? You are offering six documents which is attached to the -- your motion -- notification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which are all part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have gone through briefly those items. We find them all relevant and of probative value, and also the Chamber finds that all of them form indispensable and inseparable part of the statement, therefore, so we are admitting them all. So shall we give the exhibit number now. They will be six, so 734 to 739 in the order --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the order of the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 01511 will be 734 in terms of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you do a memo and file it for the clarity of the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a memo will be filed in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's now for you to cross-examine Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since the last topic was very emotional and understandably so, I should like to clarify a point in that regard, first of all. But before I do that, I'd like to express my condolences for your loss. All the more so -- well, I'm going to try and prove to this Court and show who committed the acts that happened on the 28th of August at Markale, and you suffered this heavy loss yourself. This isn't a question. I'd just like to express my condolences and sympathies, and I promise you that we he will show who did that and who you can blame for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I object. Expressing condolences is all very well, but the rest of the content of the accused's submission consists of argument which is best expressed in filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. Come to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. Thank you. But we have here a man who has suffered a heavy loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Crncalo at what place, or rather, where were you living on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the witness's answer. Could he repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We didn't hear the interpretation of your answer, Mr. Crncalo. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met people from Pofalic halfway up until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the question was: Where you lived at the time in August -- 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Pofalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's the distance from Pofalic to the market-place in Markale, roughly what's the distance?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up and approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Three kilometres, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, could you come closer to the microphone. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how far is it from Pofalici to Markale? You said 3 kilometres, I think.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that, since I spent 50 years living in Sarajevo, we could also count the tram stops on the way. It might be 4 kilometres, but I'll expect that -- rather 4 than 2, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I said 3 kilometres, not 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So where did you meet the man that morning who informed you about what had happened at Markale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: By the hygiene building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this hygiene building is, you mean the hygiene institute?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, hygiene institute, that's right, where he was a worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you reach that point from Pofalici? Did you go on foot?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, on foot. I didn't have any transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you meet the man by the hygiene institute?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I was walking fast, so I had much more energy than I do now and it took me about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 20 minutes from where?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: From my home to that place. I got there in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you set out?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I set out around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you met the man before half past 11.00; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So how much time did you leave -- did you need from the hygiene institute to Markale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look at my watch. I can think about it now, but I can't tell you exactly. Roughly, it took me an hour from my home, from where I lived, to the actual spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that was around 12.00; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that when you got there you found that there was nobody there, no bodies, no body parts, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any other people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, people were surprised to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody else there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: How do you mean anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you saw passers-by, and they were wondering what had happened. Did you see anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: You mean somebody filming or something like that? No, there was none of that when I came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Now, do you mean to say that at 12.00 there were no investigating organs or no officials there at all?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How close to the site were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I had to cross over -- walk through blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what did these pools of blood look like? How large were they? You said that everything was swimming in blood.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I didn't say "swimming in blood," but, yes, everything was covered in blood. As they dragged the wounded people or the people who had been killed, there were traces of blood as wide as a human body, about 10 metres on one side, 10 metres on another side. I suppose there was a car that came by to pick up these bodies from lying down in the street. So when they were dragged and moved, it was red all over. Whether it was swimming in blood or not, I don't know, but it was all red. And as I say, you could see bits of bodies, parts of clothing, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just waiting for the interpretation. Now, can you tell me who decided -- who was it who decided to drag these dead and wounded people along the street? How did that come about? You said, Yes, it was all coloured in blood, but how did these people get to be pulled across the streets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The people in Sarajevo were -- had feelings of solidarity when people were wounded and killed. They would immediately run up to these people and try and save them if they saw something like that happen. And later on I heard that, first of all, they picked up the people that first gave signs of life and brought them to Kosevo clinic. Those who gave no signs of life were taken directly to the morgue, and I suppose cars turned up. They didn't wait for any order from anybody. People went there of their own accord, trying to save anything that could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, nonetheless, Mr. Crncalo, it seems a little strange to me that somebody should drag people who are wounded or dead along the streets. I don't think this is a mark of solidarity or friendship, a gesture of friendship or solidarity in any way. I would rather say that it was hostile and unusual for people to be dragged around while they were bleeding and have their blood bleed on to the street; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I don't agree and I'll tell you why. So much had happened and so many people had been killed there, 43 people were killed there. I don't know how many were wounded exactly. But they tried -- people tried to save those people and they couldn't carry the bodies so they had to push them along or pull them along. And as to hostile, that was an enemy hostile act, that's true. But now the investigation and the measurements of everything else, this was done later on by United Nations experts to determine where the shell had come from and who had fired it. But on that day, on the day itself, nobody had any time to make any measurements or anything like that by the time I got there. Later on, United Nations experts did come to conduct an investigation to do the measurements. But when they arrived, everything had been cleared up, washed, there was just the trace of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, is it customary for investigations to be conducted after everything's been washed away and brought into some kind of order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's nothing for the witness to answer such questions. What is your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you described the action to save the people very vividly, how assistance was given and so on. How do you know when you weren't there at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, it's not difficult to imagine that it happened the way I described it. The shell had fallen as I'd heard at around 11.00, and it caused what it caused. When I arrived, that wasn't visible, but you needed some organisation and several hours to organise all this and to do the job. So that can only be done by people with feelings of solidarity, they can only be efficient in that kind of way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So during that time all the wounded and the dead were removed and what you saw were the traces of people being dragged along the streets, whether they were alive or not, and it was the blood that had splattered over the street?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That's right, but they couldn't pull them over the rail that runs along the tram tracks. And there was still some bodily -- there was still some parts of torn clothing on this railing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what would be the surface area covered in blood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I object to that question, Your Honours. It's more of a question which should be directed at one of the many investigators and those type of witnesses who investigated shell sites in Sarajevo. And it's inappropriate to burden Mr. Crncalo with this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could he not answer the question as far as he remembers or as far as he saw it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As the Court wishes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Crncalo, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't sort of take a tape measure and measure it, but I have the picture before my eyes even now. I can see it all even now. The street might have been 4 metres wide from that first -- from the first traces of where the event took place to the last. Well, about 30 metres in all, an area of about 30 metres. And where the shell fell, most of that area, that's where there was most blood. And it was about 20 metres to that area. So you can calculate it all and you can see just how much blood there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the whole width of the street was bloody, and in length it was 30 metres in one and 50 metres in another -- no, you said 20, I believe, a total of 50. So 30 metres in one direction and 20 metres in the other direction. That's what you said, I think.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Not a total of 50 metres. A total of 30 metres. So there was most blood within 30 metres. There weren't that many people over there. Whether -- well, where the shell fell, that's where it -- where the people were gathered mostly, in the middle of the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't dwell on that. Now, you went to the hospital of that. When were you at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, you know where the hospital is, you know where the event took place, so I needed more than an hour to reach the hospital. If you go on foot, I have to go down to the junction and then walk to the hospital that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I studied in that hospital and worked there for 50 years.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I know, so you should know the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I want to say is that it's much closer to Markale than Pofalici are to the hygiene institute, it's two or three times nearer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, can you imagine somebody like me seeing what I saw and not finding who I was looking for, where would I get the energy, the same energy to walk as fast as I did when I was going there? So you must take all of that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. So let's say you were at the hospital by about 1.00.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
